articles.text: There is no other way to say it—2023 started off with a bang, literally. A lightning strike destroyed a redwood sequoia on Crocker Avenue on January 10 with a divine crack that sent debris in a 100-foot radius of the event and “sounded like a bomb,” according to Resident Fran Wolfe. The lightning strike came after two weeks of heavy storms, flooding, and mudslides in the city which caused multiple road closures and fallen power lines. However, as if to offset the sudden destruction in the city, omens of creation loomed on the horizon for Piedmont. On January 19, Wickman Development & Construction began construction on the new Community Pool, a $23.8 million construction project that promised to enrich the city and provide local swimmers a central hub for the aquatics community. The Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization raised the last funds required for the project, receiving donations from local organizations and individuals. The specter of increased crime also reared its ugly head in Piedmont this year, a trend that began in January and held true over the year. Staff photos On April 6, Rosanna Bayon Moore began her role as the new City Administrator, succeeding Sara Lillevand. In 2023, construction work on the community pool created a new retaining wall and concrete foundations for its buildings among other stark visual changes. Recreation Commission voted to proceed with a five-month trial period of exclusively pickleball play at the Linda Beach Tennis Courts, with polarizing response from the community. Supporters of the trial emphasized the importance of adding play spaces to decrease wait times. Opponents criticized the decision’s abrupt nature and the lack of discussions held with neighbors of the court. City Council confirmed the hiring of Rosanna Bayon Moore as the new City Administrator at a meeting on February 21. She was to take over after the retirement of Sara Lillevand in April. At the same meeting, City Council voted to create a Climate Task Force to implement plans to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030. A 30-year-old man was pistol-whipped and shot in the wrist on February 28, one of only two shootings in Piedmont in the last decade. The victim, who was not a Piedmont resident, was transported to Highland Hospital for non-life-threatening injuries. articles.text: Was 2003 our first full year when we felt as if the pandemic was truly behind us? Or for those of us who lived through it, will it always be a memory, however dim? On occasion, spanning some three years, I wrote occasional essays titled The Pandemic Diaries. Those vignettes attempted to capture, like a snapshot, what we endured. For us, who lived through those endless months, trailing into years, upon reflection they can still seem surreal. I realize now I was often searching for an analog – a fragile comparison. What follows below is but one example. For millennia artists – writers, painters, sculptors, photographers, and more recently filmmakers – have been driven to capture their meditations on periods of extreme dislocation, suffering and uncertainty. We carry with us those images of the pandemic, many memorialized, of eerily empty streets; of gowned and shielded health care workers, their exhaustion written in their vacant stares; the haunting whisper of ventilators connected to the desperately ill; stretching lines of cars waiting at food banks; school halls and classrooms eerily silent, waiting; stores, both large and small, shuttered; refrigerator trucks idling near hospitals, shrouded in a fearful finality. We lived in the all of it, the arc of history bending toward the unknown. I recall seeing a now famous photograph taken by Dorothea Lange in 1936 at the height of the Great Depression, a period in our history often used as an analog to profound social disconnection, sustained uncertainty, deep personal loss, and economic ruination experienced by so many during the pandemic. articles.text: The Linda Beach off-leash dog area has been closed temporarily as of December 28 due to wet, slippery conditions. “Rain has saturated the hillside, causing slippery conditions, soil erosion, and unstable walking surfaces, which make the space unsafe for both dogs and pedestrians,” said the City in a press release. According to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, whether the closure will continue is based upon the weather. “Unfortunately, due to the topography of this portion of the Linda Park, the site conditions are extremely weather-dependent. Extended rain events will continue to restrict access to the off-leash portion of the park until long-term modifications occur,” said Gonzales. In the meantime, citizens may use other off-leash dog areas which remain open at the following locations: Blair Park – Entrance at Moraga Avenue between Coaches Field and Maxwelton Road Dracena Park – Entrances at the end of Artuna Avenue and 130 Dracena Avenue Piedmont Park – Entrances at 711 Highland Avenue and 305 Wildwood Avenue For status updates on the park closure, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ LindaOffLeash. articles.text: It’s the New Year – time for the annual game known as “New Year’s Resolutions.” The game goes like this. On December 31st, you make all these promises to yourself and plans. And for the first few days of January, you are, in fact, resolute – purposeful, determined, and unwavering – in those plans and promises. But by January 10 or thereabouts, real life has started up again, and with it the twists and turns of the unexpected have arrived. Can your resolutions ride those waves? Can they sustain the inevitable surprises of day-to-day existence? For most of us, the answer is NO. Research suggests that only 9% of people actually keep their New Year’s Resolutions. Which explains why the gyms across the country are packed on January 3rd and empty by January 22nd. This year, why not commit to something that is sustainable? The Creative Path is a way of walking through the world, where we allow for the discovery to be part of the journey to the destination. When you begin a creative process, you have a general sense of the outcome that you want, but the nature of a creative endeavor is that you can’t know the exact end point. So, the creative path keeps you heading in approximately the right direction, but if the path zigs when you thought it would zag, you can accept that shift as part of the journey. What does this look like in real life? Let’s use the most typical new year’s resolution, losing weight. A resolution might look like this: “I will lose 20 pounds in 2024.” Statistically, you are not likely to actually make this goal. But the creative path looks more like this, “I am exploring getting my body healthier this year through daily physical exercise that is enjoyable and fueling myself with food that makes me feel good.” With this approach, there is a much higher chance that you will follow this plan because you know what your daily work is, and you know the outcome that you are aiming towards, but it also allows for the flexibility that will be needed for long term commitment. So, as you look at your resolutions this year, maybe let go of the resolute and invite in flexibility and openness. The creative path can lead to positive outcomes and allow for the bumpy times as well. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Coach specializing in Creativity. https://gocreate. zone/

articles.text: On December 21, the last day before winter break, Coral Yeh, a Piedmont Girl Scout in Ambassador Troop 33426, held a bake sale and t-shirt sale in Piedmont Park to fundraise for Yeh’s Girl Scout Gold Award project. The Gold Award is the highest award for Girl Scouts in grades 9-12. It demonstrates extraordinary leadership in developing sustainable solutions to local, national, and global challenges that girls are personally passionate about. For her project, Yeh partnered with ocean conservation nonprofit Blue Endeavors to create a program that collects information related to ocean conditions at the Silver Bank marine area north of the Dominican Republic, a key breeding ground for humpback whales, a key species tied to the health of these ecosystems. Her program will place a buoy to collect environmental data that will be paired with whale surveying that connects ocean conditions to whale health parameters. The data from the buoy will be available on an open-source platform to be used by scientists, educators and politicians to make necessary changes for the health of the planet. This program will be available for future students to go on expeditions to collect this data and be made available through Blue Endeavors in their efforts to educate citizens of all ages on all ocean topics in the hopes of creating ocean advocates. Future students will maintain the buoy and sustain the program. Additionally, Yeh will be creating a curriculum component that will explain the biology, ecology, threats and current state of whales. The curriculum will explain how data collection works through buoys and teach audiences the important role of Humpback Whales in the overall balance of their ecosystem. This will be done using recorded discussions with experts that will be hosted on the Blue Endeavors website. The program will be accessible to scientists and politicians but also curated for educators of high school students and available to the general public. Yeh’s project needs $10,000 to purchase the Sofar data buoy that will be placed in Silver Bank Dominican Republic. The goal is to sell 333 t-shirts, available for $30 in navy or heather gray. If you would like to support the project and buy a shirt, they are $30. Those interested in helping the project may email Coral Yeh at yehcoral@gmail.com, and she will send a link to a Google form to order the shirts. Piedmont Girl Scouts Coral Yeh (right) and Sabrina Olliphant had a fundraiser in Piedmont Park on December 21 for Yeh’s Gold Award Scout project on oceanography and humpback whale health.

articles.text: Attention middle schoolers! The holidays will soon be over and you’re probably in debt for a couple presents. Your only choices are hoping your parents forgot about it or not earning an allowance any more. But wait! There is one more option - delivering the Piedmont Post. Delivering the Post is a great opportunity for you to do a few things, especially if you’re looking for a way to learn independence and reliability…and earn some money. I am a paper delivery girl and have to admit it’s not about wearing a newsboy style cap while triumphantly flinging papers that miraculously land on the middle of the door mat. Here is an easy-to-follow tip: For starters, never fling your papers, no matter how good your aim is. What will you gain? You will develop life skills and learn personal management with your earnings. I think the best part is talking to all the people you meet along the way. One interaction that sticks in my head happened when I was delivering papers to a house with a lot of steps. A man came up to me and said, “I know they are on vacation so let me take it for you.” He told me that when he was young he had a paper route. He then went on to describe how he did it. Apparently, he and a few friends used to stand on the back of a truck and tossed the papers to the houses. I told him that it sounded like fun. “Oh it was, especially the Sunday papers,” he replied. It’s connections like that that make me smile. Other things that make me smile are times like once when I was delivering a paper as soon as I turned around, the door opened and the owner said, “Thank you!” It’s the happiness of what they see in the paper and us - the people delivering them. That’s why we do it. To apply for a paper route, send an email with your name, grade in school, and your contact information to: news@piedmont-post.com.

pages.text: Thursday, January 4, 2024 7 Girl Scout fundraiser for oceanography project By Buffy Yeh On December 21, the last day before winter break, Coral Yeh, a Piedmont Girl Scout in Ambassador Troop 33426, held a bake sale and t-shirt sale in Piedmont Park to fundraise for Yeh’s Girl Scout Gold Award project. The Gold Award is the highest award for Girl Scouts in grades 9-12. It demonstrates extraordinary leadership in developing sustainable solutions to local, national, and global challenges that girls are personally passionate about. For her project, Yeh partnered with ocean conservation nonprofit Blue Endeavors to create a program that collects information related to ocean conditions at the Silver Bank marine area north of the Dominican Republic, a key breeding ground for humpback whales, a key species tied to the health of these ecosystems. Her program will place a buoy to collect environmental data that will be paired with whale surveying that connects ocean conditions to whale health parameters. The data from the buoy will be available on an open-source platform to be used by scientists, educators and politicians to make necessary changes for the health of the planet. This program will be available for future students to go on expeditions to collect this data and be made available through Blue Endeavors in their efforts to educate citizens of all ages on all ocean topics in the hopes of creating ocean advocates. Future students will maintain the buoy and sustain the program. Additionally, Yeh will be creating a curriculum component that will explain the biology, ecology, threats and current state of whales. The curriculum will explain how data collection works through buoys and teach audiences the important role of Humpback Whales in the overall balance of their ecosystem. This will be done using recorded discussions with experts that will be hosted on the Blue Endeavors website. The program will be accessible to scientists and politicians but also curated for educators of high school students and available to the general public. Yeh’s project needs $10,000 to purchase the Sofar data buoy that will be placed in Silver Bank Dominican Republic. The goal is to sell 333 t-shirts, available for $30 in navy or heather gray. If you would like to support the project and buy a shirt, they are $30. Those interested in helping the project may email Coral Yeh at yehcoral@gmail.com, and she will send a link to a Google form to order the shirts. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church dazzles community with frozen fun Photos by Michael Barber Rev. Scott Kail gives Evan Jahn a push on the tallest of two sledding hills fashioned from bales of hay and nearly 20 tons of snow. Madison Clopton enjoys a ride down the sledding hill. The usually dry parking lot of Piedmont Community Church was transformed on Friday afternoon, December 22 into a winter wonderland for the church’s firstever Snow Day. Using 20 tons of imported snow, the church created two sledding hills on the driveway from Craig Avenue to the back of the church and provided sleds for kids and adults. The free event was hosted by NextGen, PCC’s youth ministry. With an estimated 1,500 community members attending, it was an over-the-top success. “It wasn’t just kids playing,” said Kerry Persichitte, the church’s NextGen Director. “We had a lot of adults playing with their kids. We even saw Dottie Hutch, our liaison to our Senior community, going down the hill on a sled. And she’s 82!” “I think snow just really dives into our memories we may have as a child and creates this magical place where we can be a kid, no matter our age,” continued Persichitte. “We can put aside all of the other things in life and just have a little fun in nature.” Although the snow was the main attraction, two bounce houses were also on site, one gingerbread-themed and one snowman-themed. There was also free hot cocoa for children, a face painter, a balloon artist, opportunities to sing Christmas carols, a snow playground safe for toddlers for making snow angels, and building a snowman. , plus a Red Sauce Meatball food truck in the courtyard. Even Santa and his elves showed up to greet children and parents as they played in the snow. “I would say this is just the beginning,” said Persichitte. “Keep your eyes open for more similar events.” Children take advantage of the rare opportunity to make snowballs in Piedmont. Three-year-old Liam Li is thrilled by his time on the sledding hill. Two sledding hills were made in back of Piedmont Community Church Middle School students Lucy and Lauren double up on the snow tube. Santa paid a visit to the Snow Day event. The church courtyard was turned into a playground with a snow area and inflatable games and bounce houses. Nearly 20 tons of ice were transformed into snow and blown onto stacks of hay to make sledding hills. Workers from the San Jose Ice Company move ice from multiple trucks to a grinder created snow for the sledding hills.

articles.text: Each week the Piedmont Post prints excerpts from the Piedmont Police Department’s daily log, highlighting the crime items of greatest interest to residents. Some items, especially those that sound quirky, even humorous, end up being selected as the Post’s PPD Pick of the Week. The list below is a collection of our favorite PPD Picks from the year 2023. February 1 Christmas comes a little late this year. Sunday, January 22 4:40 p.m. Highland Ave. Resident reports finding laptop computer in mailbox. February 15 And what exactly seems suspicious? Monday, February 6 6:10 p.m. Mountain Ave. Report of red vehicle without headlights on stopped at stop sign, with one occupant. Vehicle gone upon officer’s arrival. Februaary 22 Is this why the cost of stamps went up again? Monday, February 13 12:36 p.m. Sandringham Rd. Report of suspicious person dressed in all black following mailman. Turns out to be postal worker supervising mail carrier. March 8 Januaury 25 A crook’s dilemma: how to ditch an empty safe Tuesday, January 17 9:46 p.m. Oakmont Ave. Residential Burglary. Safe stolen from trunk of 2019 Mercedes Benz; no forced entry made. Safe was empty. Week by week, police dispatchers are tested. . . January 11 It’s the thought that counts. Sunday, January 1 6:32 p.m. Hillside Ave. Report of seeing man and woman on property, then driving off in SUV. Officer checks home; advises that someone left a Christmas card on the door. January 18 Isn’t this a “rest” room? Monday, January 9 12:40 p.m. Highland Ave. Report of man in public restroom for 45 minutes. After knock, subject says, “wait please.” It’s a fireplace, not a car Monday, February 27 1:56 p.m. Fairview Ave. Passerby reports smoke coming from vehicle with car cover. Passerby knocks on door, but no one answers. Officers find faint odor of smoke; the source is a chimney. March 15 There’s a line around the block…days in advance. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. The Highlanders won three North Coast Section banners that day as boys’ soccer, girls’ soccer, and girls’ basketball all claimed section titles. All four winter sports varsity teams reached the NCS semifinals last winter as well, including boys’ basketball, a feat that has been rarely accomplished by small enrollment public schools. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team, the No. 8 seed, started the school’s legendary day with a 1-0 victory over No. 2 University, earning their second consecutive Div. 4 championships. They allowed no goals in postseason, winning 2-0 over No. 9 St. Helena in the first round, shocking No. 1 Cardinal Newman 1-0 in the quarterfinals, beating No. 5 Healdsburg 1-0 in the semifinals, and then upending the University Red Devils at the Beach Chalet soccer fields in Golden Gate Park. William Daniel scored the game-winning goal in the 70th minute. The girls’ soccer team, seeded No. 3, then won the NCS banner with a 2-1 win in overtime against No. 1 University on an adjacent field at Beach Chalet. It marked the team’s first section title in 20 years and coach Dan Chubbock’s first championship in his third appearance in the NCS finals. The Highlanders defeated No. 14 Sacred Heart in the opening round, bashed No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals, upset No. 2 Urban 3-0 in the semifinals, and then got the job done versus the Red Devils. Hailey Marshburn scored the game-winner against University in the 86th minute, and the players and fans celebrated the double victory on the field with the boys’ team. “It was literally back-to-backto-back. The boys’ won and we heard the girls’ basketball game’s score and I had to tell the girls to focus on our game,” said coach Chubbock. “Our game was right next to the boys’ game and you could see parents turning backand-forth to watch both games. I was texting with [girls’ basketball coach] Bryan Gardere throughout the week just wishing each other luck.” “It’s crazy. I don’t think that’s happened in my time here. Three teams winning it all? I don’t think so,” said girls’ basketball coach of over 20 years, Bryan Gardere. There were no surprises for the top-ranked girls’ basketball team winning North Coast Section as a Division 4 team. They won big, 75-49, over No. 2 Branson at Pinole Valley HS that Saturday night, claiming the school’s first section banner since 2006. The 26-point finals win over the Bulls was the closest game for the Highlanders’ during the postseason. They defeated No. 9 Lick-Wilmerding 81-29 in the quarterfinals and No. 5 McKinleyville 67-29 in the semifinals. PHS earned the highest ranking in California going into the CIF State Tournament, receiving the No. 1 seed in the Open Division. They also upset No. 5 Healdsburg 1-0 before defeating No. 2 University with a goal by William Daniel in the 70th minute. As the No. 8 seed, Piedmont became the lowest-seeded school to win an NCS title since De Anza in 2016. PHS was the lowest ranked D4 school to win the title since the divisions’ inception in 2018. The Highlanders went on to reach the Div. 4 CIF NorCal Semifinals as the No. 4 seed, where their Cinderella season came to a close on March 2 with a 4-0 loss to No. 1 ranked Marin Academy. Earlier Piedmont defeated No. 5 Kimball 2-0 on February 28. Enzo Bernales led the boys’ team and was named Sophomore of the Year by the Post. Girls Soccer lifts first banner in 20 years The girls’ soccer team finished with a 13-1-6 (W-T-L) record and won its first D4 banner in two decades. As the No. 3 seed, Piedmont upset No. 1 University 2-1 for the title on February 25 with a Golden Goal in the 86th minute of overtime by Hailey Marshburn to win the school’s first NCS banner since 2003. To get there, PHS shut out No. 2 Urban of San Francisco 3-0l on February 22 in the semifinals and bashed No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals on February 18. They opened the postseason with a 2-0 win over No. 15 Sacred Heart on February 15. Advancing to the Division 3 CIF NorCal Regional Tournament, No. 8 ranked Piedmont nearly upset No. 1 Sequoia in the first round on February 28, but lost 2-1 in sudden-death overtime. Soccer stars Audrey Lam and Emily Fitzgerald were named Honorable Mention by the Post as Athlete of the Year. Lam’s impact as a maestro in the midfield was easy to see—

Trinity Zamora closed her high school career in an exclusive club with over 2,000 points and 1,400 total rebounds. She is one of the most accomplished four-year starters in PHS history. She now plays at San Diego State. A.J. Harris all-time leading scorer A.J. Harris finished his illustrious Piedmont High career as the school’s all-time leading scorer with 1,570 points. He accomplished this in just two full varsity seasons and an abbreviated 2021 season due to COVID. Harris was named the WACC’s Co-Player of the Year alongside Berkeley’s Samir O’Brien. The Highlanders went 19-10 with Harris carrying the load as the team’s leading scorer and rebounder. They made it to the Division 3 NCS Semifinals as the No. 4 seed before losing to No. 1 Branson, 61-40 on February 21. Earlier PHS beat No. 5 Analy 59-38 in the quarterfinals on February 17 and beat No. 13 Rancho Cotate 65-43 in the opening round on February 14. Harris scored 28 points in the semifinals against the Bulls and 37 on Analy to eclipse the all-time mark. He scored over 30 points six times last season, including a high of 37 against Division 3 State Champions, Oakland High. He now plays at Emory University. Parker Long among best halfmilers Parker Long concluded his track career at Piedmont and was among the best to ever run the 800 meters. He graduates with the third fastest time in school history at 1:53.25, set at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18. His time placed him narrowly behind some of PHS track royalty, including The Posts’ 2018 Athlete of the Year, Reece Proctor, and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer, Gordon Johnson, while finishing .15 ahead of teammate from last year, Cooper Downing. articles.text: Aurora Theater in Berkeley is presenting Mary Kathryn Nagle’s Manhatta, a gripping journey from the fur trade of the 1600s to the stock trade of today. Performances are scheduled from Tuesday, March 5 through March 10, with a live-streamed performance online. Directed by Shannon R. Davis, Manhatta tells the story of a young Lenape woman, Jane Snake, who returns to her ancestral homeland, “Manahatta,” with a Stanford MBA to work as a securities trader on Wall Street — the once-walled street built by enslaved Africans to keep the indigenous Lenape out. Set mainly against the backdrop of the Occupy Wall Street movement across centuries, Manahatta draws parallels between the forced removal, taxation, and the fiscal impact on Native Americans during the 2008 financial crisis and the 1626 Dutch purchase of the island of “Manahatta,” or Manhattan. Playwright Nagle, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, teases the duality in Jane as she seeks to uncover her complicity in infrastructure designed to destroy her people. Throughout the play, deemed “fascinating and provocative” by the New Haven Review, Jane’s career is thriving on “the island of many hills” (Manahatta in Lenape). Back home in Oklahoma her mother and sister are grieving the loss of family, and struggling to maintain their culture, language, and their finances to stay in their over-mortgaged home. Come join the Aurora Theatre for a discussion of its production after the show on any of four dates: Friday, February 16; Tuesday, February 20; Wednesday, February 27; and Thursday, March 7. Everyone is welcome to join Aurora Theater for Native Community Night during the Friday, February 23 production for a preshow reception at 6 p.m. and a post-show discussion following the 8 p.m. show. Showtime information and tickets ($35–$40) are available at the Box Office at 843-4822 or online at tickets.auroratheatre. org. Aurora Theater is located at 2081 Addison Street in Berkeley. Mary Kathryn Nagle’s Manhatta premieres at Berkeley’s Aurora Theatre, opening on Friday, February 9, with performances through March 10.

articles.text: Catch the world premiere of Kate Attwell’s play Big Data, directed by Tony Award winner Pam MacKinnon, at San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater from Thursday, February 15 through March 10. Do our devices – tantalizingly incarnate in this funny, uncanny world premiere – really know us best? Are our digital footprints predictive of our future choices, or are they choosing for us? In the play the protagonist Sam loves Timmy, and Lucy loves Max, but the pressures of modern life leave them anxious, lonely, and susceptible to the siren song of tech. When Sam and Lucy’s parents make a shocking announcement, the family is forced to confront what’s distracted them from each other – and the legacy they’ll leave behind. ACT Artistic Director MacKinnon and playwright Attwell reunite to realize this revolutionary piece, inspired by Attwell’s experience touring Mozilla’s “Glass Room” pop-up interactive exhibit in San Francisco. Come explore questions of attention, connection, nourishment, and the dizzying possibilities of AI. “Kate Attwell has written a play so topical about how AI is rapidly and maybe forever changing how we interact and think about what we want,” said MacKinnon. “I love Kate’s voice as a playwright, her surprising humor and mischief, and all she throws into and at her characters. I feel grateful that this is our second world premiere production together at A.C.T. and hold fond memories of [our previous collaboration] Testmatch in 2019. I am also grateful that while the Bay and the world wrestle with the fundamental ethics of where we are headed, that this play is in the wrestle too.” Come to the theater on Friday, February 16 at 6:30 p.m. for a party before the show with a DJ and drinks, On Tuesday, February 27 at 7 p.m.; Sunday, March 3 at 2 p.m.; and Wednesday, March 6 at 2 p.m., stick around after the show for a lively question-and-answer session with the actors and artists behind the work. Information about showtimes, more related events and tickets ($25–$130) for the play at ACT’s Toni Rembe Theater (415 Geary St., San Francisco) are available at the ACT Theater Box Office at 415-749-2228 or online at act-sf. org/bigdata. articles.text: The first major West Coast exhibition of South African visual artist Zanele Muholi will be on view at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art from January 18 through August 11, 2024. The exhibition, titled Zanele Muholi: Eye Me, brings together over 100 of the artist’s photographs from 2002 to the present, alongside paintings, sculpture and video, providing an opportunity for audiences to experience Muholi’s expansive artistic project to celebrate and make visible black and LGBT self-expression in post-Apartheid South Africa. A self-described visual activist using photography as a tool for resistance and social change, Muholi’s work includes issues of representation, race and the dangers of being true to one’s gender identity and culture in South Africa. Muholi’s work calls attention to the violence enacted on LGBT people while also celebrating their bravery, beauty and resilience. With a sense of profound tenderness, Muholi’s portraiture is distinguished by an intimacy that could only be established through trust. The artist sees subjects as collaborators who partake in the process of creating the images, from the selection of the location to the clothing. SFMOMA, located at 151 3rd Street in San Francisco, is open from 10 a.m. through 5 p.m. Zanele Muholi, Faniswa, Seapoint, Cape Town, 2016. articles.text: Showtime information and tickets ($29-$495) for the performance at War Memorial Opera House (301 Van Ness Avenue) are available at the SF Ballet Box Artistic Director Tamara Rojo launches the 2024 season of SF Ballet with an immersive performance of Mere Mortals from Friday, January 26 through February 1. Music and dance converge in a singular environment of mesmerizing light and video. The new ballet with music by composer Floating Points and choreography from Aszure Barton, contextualizes the ancient parable of Pandora’s Box for the current technological world. In the ancient Greek myth of Pandora’s Jar, Pandora is the first woman on earth created by the gods to serve humanity. She’s given a jar as a gift and instructed not to open it under any circumstances. When curiosity gets the better of her, she opens the jar, releasing all the evils and miseries into the world. Only hope remains trapped inside. While the ballet’s narrative dates to the first centuries of humanity, there are parallels found in contemporary society today, including unintended consequences of technology, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), and ethical dilemmas in science and technology. The work’s dramaturgist Carmen Kovacs said, “We started with the original myth, but since it has been changed and interpreted in so many ways, we thought we would do our own story and combine it with this idea of AI and how humankind has brought it upon themselves.” Ballerina Jennifer Stahl and San Francisco Ballet members rehearsing Aszure Barton’s and Sam Shepherd’s Mere Mortals, which will have its world premiere on Friday, January 26.
articles.title: Mere Mortals world premiere at SF Ballet opens Jan. 26

articles.text: There is a stillness in the air and the streets are almost devoid of traffic. The cold winter sun casts long shadows. The Christmas rush is over as the old year raced towards its inevitable close. Observations like this cause us to reflect on the year past. Generally speaking, our thoughts depend on our outlook on life. A certain overindulgence causes most of us to make New Year’s resolutions. While some of the world has gone into artistic hibernation, others have found ways to be productive. A talented musical friend of mine has written five books on violin technique. He claims that these books are his musical autobiography. There is no doubt that he has lived a full life and the books are proof of that. For some musical organizations, Spring has come early. Both San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera have a new Music Director. Oakland Symphony continues its search for a luminary to illuminate the podium. On the home front, the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is planning some exciting concerts. The Piedmont Center for the Arts continues on its successful course despite some roadblocks instigated by politicians and petty bureaucrats. On a personal note, my wife and I enjoyed a New Year’s Eve feast last year at one of our favorite restaurants, Italian Colors. The festive spirit was everywhere despite the storm… um, I mean… The atmospheric river. We enjoyed superb prawns stuffed with Dungeness crab on the first official day of San Francisco’s crab season one year ago. A unique pizza topped with fragrant black truffles was not exactly Neapolitan, but it was memorable nevertheless. Adding to the evening’s enjoyment was a visit to the table by the restaurant owner Alan Carlson and his son Dylan who stopped by to give us extra slices of both black and white truffles. A lively couple at the neighboring table brought over some of their prize-winning wine and aged brandy. As the Germans say. “Das leben ist Lebenswert (literally, “life is beautiful”). As the “atmospheric river” continues on its way to the sea at the start of 2024, whether you ask the question in singular “quo vadis”, or make it more general in the plural, “quo vadimus” (where are we going?), we ask, has anything changed? Have a great year.
articles.title: Winter thoughts

articles.text: “We are experiencing an entertainment revolution” The 81st Golden Globes annual awards ceremony will take place on Jan. 7, 2024, at the Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills and will air live on CBS from 5-8 p.m. It will honor the Best in films and television from the past year. The list of nominees was recently posted. The Globe Awards were the creation of the Hollywood Foreign Press Association in 1944, and today is comprised of 300 international journalists who cover the American entertainment industry. In many respects its annual awards ceremony mirrors the Oscars (to include the runway glitterati, brief interviews, formal wear and haute couture) with one increasingly important difference – the unexpectedly prescient category titled Television. The Oscars, founded in 1927, continues to be Hollywood’s most prestigious artistic award ceremony in the film industry. Winners are selected by the nearly 10,000-person membership of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Science. Its list of nominations will soon be announced in anticipation of its 96th annual gala in early March 2024 and is slated to air on ABC. For decades the inclusion of television likely placed the ceremony in a tier just below the Oscars. To watch TV was, well, pedestrian. Film was something else. Since the early 1900s, there have been larger-than-life big screens. And the grainy, flickering films, silent at first, soon included sound, the photography became more vivid (recall the advent of Technicolor), dialogue more graphic, and plots more intense, some driven by special effects technology such as CGI. Movies soon took audiences to places that were and are extraordinary. To watch Top Gun for the first time was unforgettable. After almost a century the experience of going to the movies has become deeply embedded in our culture. The actors were called “stars,” and for countless fans the line between the fiction on the screen and the reality that awaited them upon leaving the theater was often blurred. Film became and remains entertainment like no other – both evocative and emotive. And then came the COVID pandemic and we found ourselves confined for long periods in our homes. As theaters closed and movie sets shut down, it quickly became evident to Hollywood that audiences regarded sitting in a dark, cavernous room with strangers to watch a movie as high risk. Lock-downs were mandated, streets eerily empty, masks and vaccines debated. As a nation, we were haunted by this invisible virus. And so we waited and turned to our televisions, watching anything that was entertaining or newsworthy. Those of us who hadn’t yet discovered Netflix and similar streaming services, learned that thousands of movies were available as well as enormous wall-mounted screens that offered state-of-the-art clarity and sound. Not only were previously released films accessible, but Netflix, Paramount+, Prime and Disney+ began making their own films and signing name actors. It became clear that many of these movies did not adhere to the standard two-hour format. What became available were lengthy series, identified by seasons and episodes. This new configuration allowed writers to develop far more complex characters, create evolving, expanding plots, increasingly diverse settings, and multiple, simultaneous story lines. A season can end (not conclude) with the promise that the story line will continue, opening later with, say, Season 2-Episode 1. If an episode is missed, it’s easy to find and watch it. If a series is newly discovered, you can start at the beginning and binge-watch. If the series proves compelling, you can wait several weeks then rinse and repeat. Meanwhile, there is always a long list of traditional movies offered on various sites such as Freevee, Hallmark, Tubi or YouTube, featuring long-ago released films now available. Which brings us back to the Golden Globes, and the “Best of“ television categories (12), derived from streaming formats, There’s “Best Television Series – Drama”; “Best Television Series – “Musical or Comedy”; “Best Television Limited Series, Anthology Series, or Motion Picture Made for Television.” Examples would be the series 1923, 1893, Yellowstone, The Crown, Jack Ryan, Bosch, or The Lincoln Lawyer. And many more, with A-list actors and superb writing. It is with these categories, many made especially for streaming on television, that the Golden Globes has become more relevant to that growing post-pandemic audience that now prefers to be entertained watching newly released series or traditional movies from the comfort of their sofas or easy chairs instead of going to a movie theater. I would suggest that we are experiencing an entertainment revolution, one that is still evolving. It is the Golden Globes that finds itself ahead of the curve, while the Academy Awards, which is focused solely on film, will either adapt or become a niche ceremony with a shrinking audience. I realize that it’s hard to imagine that movie theaters will one day be viewed with head-shaking nostalgia. Of course, I could be wrong. These places, with their giant screens and Dolby sound, will not go the way of the landline. We’ll see.
articles.title: THE FUTURE OF MOVIES The Golden Globes and the Academy Awards

articles.text: Tianna Sansbury, Laura Monagan and Everlyn Sampi in Rabbit-Proof Fence Review by Chris Honoré Rabbit-Proof Fence is an extraordinary and surprising film, not only in its austere, Australian location, but in its focus. The story, set in 1931, is adapted from the novel Follow the Rabbit-Proof Fence by Doris Pilkington, and recounts the journey of three young girls – Molly (Evelyn Sampi), Daisy (Tianna Scansbury), and Gracie (Laura Monaghan). They are, to use a softer Hawaiian word, “hapa.” One parent is white and the other is Aborigine (the indigenous people of Australia). They are referred to as “half-castes.” During this period it was Australia’s policy to take these hapa children from their parents, forcibly when necessary, and send them to Christian orphanages cum schools where they would become “civilized.” Some would be placed with families as maids, others were married off to a white male with the intention that after three generations the dark color of their skin would vanish along with all remnants of their culture. In Rabbit-Proof Fence the government official charged with reeducating the kidnapped children is called, simply, Mr. Neville (Kenneth Branagh). He is blind to the racism in his views and the cruelty inflicted not only on the defenseless children but on their parents. And therein is the essence of this film. Molly (14), Daisy (10), and Gracie (8) are taken by train to one such orphanage; however, instead of bending to the harsh rules, with Molly in charge, they plan their escape and set off into the outback, determined to return home to Jigalong, where their mothers live. What they are unaware of is that they are 1200 miles away, and uncertain how they will survive or possibly find their way. And thus begins their journey across a desiccated, unforgiving land. While they meet local ranchers/farmers along the way, they find that some are momentarily helpful, and others are hostile, carriers of attitudes born of prejudice and discrimination. The three are unaware that an Aboriginal tracker, Moodoo (David Gulpili), on horseback, has been hired by the orphanage to find the girls and bring them back. He is not far behind. Molly soon realizes that if they follow the endlessly long Rabbit-Proof Fence they will eventually come to Jigalong and there be reunited with their mothers. Meanwhile, Neville has hired his own searchers, and is certain that the girls are indeed using the Fence as a kind of compass. Studying maps of the area, he intends to intercept them before they reach home. Rabbit-Proof Fence is wonderful story of courage, defiance, and determination. The photography, the images of these three girls as they struggle find their way, are stunning and their performances, especially that of Evelyn Sampi as Molly, are touching and heartfelt. pages.text: 20 Thursday, January 4, 2024 THE FUTURE OF MOVIES The Golden Globes and the Academy Awards “We are experiencing an entertainment revolution” By Chris Honoré The 81st Golden Globes annual awards ceremony will take place on Jan. 7, 2024, at the Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills and will air live on CBS from 5-8 p.m. It will honor the Best in films and television from the past year. The list of nominees was recently posted. The Globe Awards were the creation of the Hollywood Foreign Press Association in 1944, and today is comprised of 300 international journalists who cover the American entertainment industry. In many respects its annual awards ceremony mirrors the Oscars (to include the runway glitterati, brief interviews, formal wear and haute couture) with one increasingly important difference – the unexpectedly prescient category titled Television. The Oscars, founded in 1927, continues to be Hollywood’s most prestigious artistic award ceremony in the film industry. Winners are selected by the nearly 10,000-person membership of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Science. Its list of nominations will soon be announced in anticipation of its 96th annual gala in early March 2024 and is slated to air on ABC. For decades the inclusion of television likely placed the ceremony in a tier just below the Oscars. To watch TV was, well, pedestrian. Film was something else. Since the early 1900s, there have been larger-than-life big screens. And the grainy, flickering films, silent at first, soon included sound, the photography became more vivid (recall the advent of Technicolor), dialogue more graphic, and plots more intense, some driven by special effects technology such as CGI. Movies soon took audiences to places that were and are extraordinary. To watch Top Gun for the first time was unforgettable. After almost a century the experience of going to the movies has become deeply embedded in our culture. The actors were called “stars,” and for countless fans the line between the fiction on the screen and the reality that awaited them upon leaving the theater was often blurred. Film became and remains entertainment like no other – both evocative and emotive. And then came the COVID pandemic and we found ourselves confined for long periods in our homes. As theaters closed and movie sets shut down, it quickly became evident to Hollywood that audiences regarded sitting in a dark, cavernous room with strangers to watch a movie as high risk. Lock-downs were mandated, streets eerily empty, masks and vaccines debated. As a nation, we were haunted by this invisible virus. And so we waited and turned to our televisions, watching anything that was entertaining or newsworthy. Those of us who hadn’t yet discovered Netflix and similar streaming services, learned that thousands of movies were available as well as enormous wall-mounted screens that offered state-of-the-art clarity and sound. Not only were previously released films accessible, but Netflix, Paramount+, Prime and Disney+ began making their own films and signing name actors. It became clear that many of these movies did not adhere to the standard two-hour format. What became available were lengthy series, identified by seasons and episodes. This new configuration allowed writers to develop far more complex characters, create evolving, expanding plots, increasingly diverse settings, and multiple, simultaneous story lines. A season can end (not conclude) with the promise that the story line will continue, opening later with, say, Season 2-Episode 1. If an episode is missed, it’s easy to find and watch it. If a series is newly discovered, you can start at the beginning and binge-watch. If the series proves compelling, you can wait several weeks then rinse and repeat. Meanwhile, there is always a long list of traditional movies offered on various sites such as Freevee, Hallmark, Tubi or YouTube, featuring long-ago released films now available. Which brings us back to the Golden Globes, and the “Best of“ television categories (12), derived from streaming formats, There’s “Best Television Series – Drama”; “Best Television Series – “Musical or Comedy”; “Best Television Limited Series, Anthology Series, or Motion Picture Made for Television.” Examples would be the series 1923, 1893, Yellowstone, The Crown, Jack Ryan, Bosch, or The Lincoln Lawyer. And many more, with A-list actors and superb writing. It is with these categories, many made especially for streaming on television, that the Golden Globes has become more relevant to that growing post-pandemic audience that now prefers to be entertained watching newly released series or traditional movies from the comfort of their sofas or easy chairs instead of going to a movie theater. I would suggest that we are experiencing an entertainment revolution, one that is still evolving. It is the Golden Globes that finds itself ahead of the curve, while the Academy Awards, which is focused solely on film, will either adapt or become a niche ceremony with a shrinking audience. I realize that it’s hard to imagine that movie theaters will one day be viewed with head-shaking nostalgia. Of course, I could be wrong. These places, with their giant screens and Dolby sound, will not go the way of the landline. We’ll see. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Democracy is not a spectator sport! MOVIE FOR KIDS Rabbit-Proof Fence Tianna Sansbury, Laura Monagan and Everlyn Sampi in Rabbit-Proof Fence Review by Chris Honoré Rabbit-Proof Fence is an extraordinary and surprising film, not only in its austere, Australian location, but in its focus. The story, set in 1931, is adapted from the novel Follow the Rabbit-Proof Fence by Doris Pilkington, and recounts the journey of three young girls – Molly (Evelyn Sampi), Daisy (Tianna Scansbury), and Gracie (Laura Monaghan). They are, to use a softer Hawaiian word, “hapa.” One parent is white and the other is Aborigine (the indigenous people of Australia). They are referred to as “half-castes.” During this period it was Australia’s policy to take these hapa children from their parents, forcibly when necessary, and send them to Christian orphanages cum schools where they would become “civilized.” Some would be placed with families as maids, others were married off to a white male with the intention that after three generations the dark color of their skin would vanish along with all remnants of their culture. In Rabbit-Proof Fence the government official charged with reeducating the kidnapped children is called, simply, Mr. Neville (Kenneth Branagh). He is blind to the racism in his views and the cruelty inflicted not only on the defenseless children but on their parents. And therein is the essence of this film. Molly (14), Daisy (10), and Gracie (8) are taken by train to one such orphanage; however, instead of bending to the harsh rules, with Molly in charge, they plan their escape and set off into the outback, determined to return home to Jigalong, where their mothers live. What they are unaware of is that they are 1200 miles away, and uncertain how they will survive or possibly find their way. And thus begins their journey across a desiccated, unforgiving land. While they meet local ranchers/farmers along the way, they find that some are momentarily helpful, and others are hostile, carriers of attitudes born of prejudice and discrimination. The three are unaware that an Aboriginal tracker, Moodoo (David Gulpili), on horseback, has been hired by the orphanage to find the girls and bring them back. He is not far behind. Molly soon realizes that if they follow the endlessly long Rabbit-Proof Fence they will eventually come to Jigalong and there be reunited with their mothers. Meanwhile, Neville has hired his own searchers, and is certain that the girls are indeed using the Fence as a kind of compass. Studying maps of the area, he intends to intercept them before they reach home. Rabbit-Proof Fence is wonderful story of courage, defiance, and determination. The photography, the images of these three girls as they struggle find their way, are stunning and their performances, especially that of Evelyn Sampi as Molly, are touching and heartfelt. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group has a standing joke that it never rains in Piedmont on Wednesday mornings. Their lucky charm was broken on December 20 when a small group gathered in the rain with their umbrellas at the Exedra: Lisa Euphrat, Jim Kellogg, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Charlene Louie, Sherry Jacobs, Pat Keller, Priscilla Wanerus, and Dick Carter. An additional 13 walkers showed up for the group’s annual holiday luncheon at Zachary’s Pizza on Grand Avenue. That group included Christine Calliste, Aaron Katzel. Rob Smith, Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado, David Haecker, Elizabeth Richter, Chuck Oraftik, Alicia Rivera, Brenda Ferrero, Harriette Louie, Mike and Nancy Henn. As they passed the recently closed Piedmont Shell Station, its history and current status were shared. Piedmont Shell had been in Piedmont for 95 years, but it was announced in November that it would close at end of the month. The property is being sold by Shell Auto Care owner Jeff Hansen to Shell Recharge, a division of Shell Oil. The station has three 10,000-gallon gas tanks under the pumps that need to be replaced by 2025. New tanks would have enabled the station to continue to sell gas for decades, but the increased popularity of electric vehicles made the owner feel uncomfortable with the future of gasoline stations and the investment. Influencing this was California’s plans to achieve 100% new zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035, and have a 25% reduction in smog-causing pollution by 2037. Shell plans to demolish the existing station and replace it with a 14-bay electric vehicle charging hub under the Shell Recharge brand. Fast charging will be provided with power up to 360kW. Pricing of charges will be on a pay-as-you-go basis with prices on an app, and varying base on the time of day. No employees will be regularly on the site. These plans need permitting and regulatory approval. Shell hopes the project will be added to the City’s public hearing January agenda, and that they will be able to start construction in the first half of 2024. She promised to start a Wednesday walking group in Granada. articles.text: It is never too soon to be proactive about your health and longevity. As we ring in the New Year, many of us have considered that healthy lifestyle goals and the meals we consume are a large part of it. Gigantic Royal Corona beans are the stars of this soup. They cook up tender and, dare I say, “meaty” owing to their size and toothsomeness. They’re as fun to eat as they are impressive to those new to them. Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup Adapted from Diane Kochilas’ Fasolada – Bean Soup with Pumpkin & Corn Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • 1/2 pound giant beans such as Royal Corona or Greek gigantes • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided, preferably Greek • 1-1/2 red onion, coarsely chopped, about 1-1/2 cups • 2 tablespoons fresh garlic, minced, divided • 1 tablespoon tomato paste • 1 14.5 ounce can diced tomatoes • 1 bay leaf • 1/2 teaspoon dried oregano, or 2 sprigs fresh • 1 3-inch-long strip of fresh orange peel • 1 cup corn kernels • 1 cup cubed delicata or butternut squash • 1/4 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped • 1 – 2 teaspoons honey, preferably local • 1 tablespoon balsamic vinegar, scant measure to taste • 1/2 – 1 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • A few grinds black peppercorns, to taste INSTRUCTIONS Check the beans for debris, rinse and then soak overnight; drain and discard the soaking water. Soaking is optional but will decrease the cooking time considerably. Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large soup pot over medium heat. Add the red onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 5–10 minutes. Stir occasionally to prevent scorching. Stir in 1 tablespoon of the minced garlic (set remaining 1 tablespoon aside for later), give it a quick stir; then add the tomato paste. Stir again to incorporate the tomato paste well. Add the drained beans, canned tomatoes, bay leaf, oregano, and orange peel. Top off with enough water to cover by 2 inches. Bring to a boil then reduce to a simmer until the beans are very tender, about 1-1/2 to 2 hours. When the beans are tender, scoop out about 1 cup of the soup and puree in a food processor or blender/immersion stick blender, then return to the pot. This blending step is optional but will add a bit of body to the soup. Meanwhile, heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Cook the squash and corn until lightly browned, then add the remaining garlic and sea salt. Mix well then add to the soup pot once the beans have cooked through and the pureed portion has been added back to the pot. Return the soup to a simmer and adjust the seasoning with additional salt and black pepper. Just before serving remove the orange peel and bay leaf. Stir in the chopped parsley, honey and balsamic vinegar. Serve with an additional drizzle of high-quality, extra-virgin olive oil and a few sprinkles of parsley. articles.text: Penelope “Penny” Knowland Robb of Piedmont, a friend and colleague of many in town for many years, passed away on January 1, 2024. She was 79. Born in Seattle, Washington on March 1, 1944, she was the daughter of Joseph Russell Knowland, Jr. and Norma Diane Piva, She graduated from Piedmont High School in 1961 and in 1991 she graduated from the University of California, Berkeley with her bachelor’s degree in social sciences. Penny married Orland “Dean” Robb, Sr. on July 21, 1962, in Piedmont Community Church. They lived in Columbia, Missouri for a year before settling in Piedmont. They lived on Hillside Avenue for almost 30 years where they enjoyed countless neighborhood block parties, family celebrations, and domino tournaments. Penny and Dean had 40 wonderful years together before his death in February 2002. Penny worked as a Supervisor in the Piedmont Recreation Department for 30 years before retiring in December 2014. Many Piedmonters booked the Community Center or Veterans Hall through her. She was an active member of the Piedmont community and served as a member of the Piedmont Community Church, the Piedmont Fortnightly Book Club, the Piedmont Historical Society, and the Piedmont Seniors group. She was a life-long volunteer of the UCSF Benioff Children’s her love of baseball and travel. She was an A’s season ticket holder for over 40 years and recently worked for the A’s organization as a secretary to the owner. In November 2023, she took her family to Yosemite National Park. It was her first time going to Yosemite and it will be a fond memory for her family. articles.text: We are saddened to announce that H. Ellison Dunlap Jr., a long time member of the Piedmont Highlander Drums and Pipes band, passed away on October 24, 2023. Ellison was born on January 4, 1944 and raised in Salt Lake City, Utah. He attended classes at the University of Utah and moved to Alameda, California with his mother as a young man. He worked for Montgomery Ward as a display artist and photographer and served two years as a Mormon missionary in Wales, where he met his wife, Nancy. He and Nancy founded their printing business, West Coast Arts, in the late 1960’s. After a long career in printing, health issues forced him to retire. Ellison led a full life with numerous hobbies and businesses. He was an award-winning professional photographer, amateur historian, and also won awards as an amateur filmmaker. He headed the Social Committee for the Concord Gun Club, served as a teacher in his church, and shared his artistic talents in support of many church events. He was a member of numerous historical reenactment groups, including Roman, Medieval, Renaissance, Civil War, and WWII. He had a wide-ranging collection of militaria and loved to dress up in period outfits. He excelled in blacksmithing, ceramics, cooking, drawing, garden railroading, jewelry making, magic, mold-making, photography, sculpting, sewing, and ventriloquism. He also played the accordion and was a drummer in the Piedmont Highlander Drums and Pipes band. What wave of harshness brought her to this moment? And if her gaze is lost in another place – perhaps filled with memories of where she began, or of thoughts about where this journey might end – then her emotions are clearly defined by an unrelenting uncertainty. Her moment is the Great Depression, an economic riptide that swept millions of Americans away, a time made manifest by breadlines, shanty towns, desperate men and women lost, their experiences to be etched forever in their memories, a referent voiced forever as before and after. The images from the Depression are vastly different from ours; yet, in many ways, they are the same. Our neighborhoods were silent, doors closed, drapes tightly drawn, families, friends, perhaps strangers waiting inside. Unspeaking masked shoppers walked apart, stood in hushed lines in grocery stores and pharmacies, waiting to pay, taking creased bills in change, wondering where they had been before, whose hands they had passed through. Everywhere the floors were marked with small red admonishments to keep one’s distance. How close was too close? Even the hint of a greeting smile was lost behind cloth. Is this the new normal, we grimly wondered? Or will this, the all of it, be our before and after, sometimes, always, remembered?

A rest stop, if only for a night? What wave of harshness brought her to this moment? And if her gaze is lost in another place – perhaps filled with memories of where she began, or of thoughts about where this journey might end – then her emotions are clearly defined by an unrelenting uncertainty. Her moment is the Great Depression, an economic riptide that swept millions of Americans away, a time made manifest by breadlines, shanty towns, desperate men and women lost, their experiences to be etched forever in their memories, a referent voiced forever as before and after. The images from the Depression are vastly different from ours; yet, in many ways, they are the same. Our neighborhoods were silent, doors closed, drapes tightly drawn, families, friends, perhaps strangers waiting inside. Unspeaking masked shoppers walked apart, stood in hushed lines in grocery stores and pharmacies, waiting to pay, taking creased bills in change, wondering where they had been before, whose hands they had passed through. Everywhere the floors were marked with small red admonishments to keep one’s distance. How close was too close? Even the hint of a greeting smile was lost behind cloth. Is this the new normal, we grimly wondered? Or will this, the all of it, be our before and after, sometimes, always, remembered?
